newsitem.title: USA: Watchdog group says Clinton, Dole camps broke law.
newsitem.headline: Watchdog group says Clinton, Dole camps broke law.

text.p: A non-profit campaign watchdog group charged Tuesday that both the 1996 campaigns of President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole broke the law and should be investigated by a special prosecutor.
Officials of Common Cause told a news conference that Attorney General Janet Reno was wrong last week in turning down demands to seek an independent counsel to look into financing irregularities.

Common Cause president Ann McBride and the group's lawyer, Fred Wertheimer, argued that Reno based her rejection in part on an incorrect analysis by Justice Department lawyers that many television ads were financed with "soft money" not subject to federal campaign law restrictions.

McBride said "the Clinton and Dole presidential campaigns, using their parties as conduits, raised and spent millions of dollars during the 1996 election for TV advertising campaigns, in violation of the Federal Election Campaign Act."

The group insisted that millions of dollars in "soft money" from corporations and others were funnelled to the Democratic and Republican Parties but controlled improperly by the Clinton and Dole campaigns against federal law.

Steve Langdon, a spokesman for the Democratic National Committee, did not respond directly to Common Cause's charges but said the party "has raised and spent hard and soft money according to the requirements of the law." It had joined Common Cause and other reform groups in calling for changes including a ban on raising and spending of soft money by national party committees."

While candidates are restricted in what they can raise from individuals and political action committees, parties -- not candidates or their campaign committees -- can raise vast amounts of unrestricted "soft money" for general party building activities.

"While the money solicited and spent by the Clinton and Dole presidential campaigns was technically deposited into and disbursed out of political party bank accounts, the political parties in reality only played a clerical role regarding these funds," McBride said.
"The parties simply served as conduits for the presidential campaigns," she said.
"Simply labeling a contribution or expenditures as soft money does not make it so," she added.

McBride said "both campaigns went around the law to go and use the political parties as conduits, to raise money that was illegal and to spend money that was illegal and that's what it looks like on the public record."

Instead of setting in motion the process for naming an independent counsel, or special prosecutor, Reno decided to continue her own Justice Department investigation into reported charges of improper fund-raising, mainly involving the Clinton campaign.
Her decision was met with an angry reaction from her Republican critics in Congress demanding a special prosecutor.

In addition to the Justice Department probe, two congressional committees are investigating reports that Democratic fund-raisers raised money illegally or improperly from foreign sources and enticed contributors with White House coffees with Clinton and other perks.
Last October, Common Cause urged Reno to name an independent counsel. Other calls have come from Republican sin Congress but she has rebuffed the requests.
Since then, Common Cause said new information had come to light, including a book by former Clinton adviser Dick Morris, that shed more light on fund-raising and televison ads.
